title: Fewshot contrasts & nullspace lab notes
content:
Purpose: quick scratchpad to capture experiments mixing contrastive few-shot exemplars with explicit 'nullspace' anchors. Trying to make prompts resilient to instruction drift and token-budget brittle cases.

High-level idea:
- Contrast sets: give paired positive/negative exemplars (not just class labels) so model sees what to do and what NOT to do.
- Nullspace anchors: short exemplars that map certain inputs to an explicit empty/NO-OP output to teach a model to withhold when conditions not met (useful for hallucination control).
- Token-budget microtemplates: compact few-shot templates that preserve contrast while staying sub-200 token budget.

Open questions / hypotheses:
- Hypothesis 1: pairing negative exemplars reduces false-positive extra-info hallucinations in open-ended summarization tasks.
- Hypothesis 2: nullspace exemplars increase precision at the cost of some recall; tunable via soft vs hard anchors.
- Experiment question: how many negative exemplars before we see diminishing returns? 1 vs 3 vs 5.

Quick experiments (notes):
1) Base microtemplate (2-shot, positive only) — baseline for recall/fluency.
Prompt: "You are a concise assistant. Summarize the article in one sentence. Only include facts stated in the text."
Few-shot pairs: (P1, P2) short examples.
Result: high recall, but occasional invented specifics when input ambiguous.

2) Contrast microtemplate (1 pos + 1 neg)
Instruction: same. Exemplars: one good summary, one counterexample where the summary incorrectly adds an invented figure and the correct output is "No additional facts can be inferred."
Observation: model less likely to invent numeric specifics, but sometimes becomes overly conservative (drops useful implied facts).

3) Nullspace anchor (explicit suppression exemplar)
- Include exemplar: input that is clearly underspecified -> expected output explicitly: "NO_SUMMARY_NEEDED" (or a short phrase).
- Use both soft anchor (natural phrase) and hard-coded token (NO_SUMMARY_NEEDED) — compare.
Result: hard token anchor is more effective at suppressing hallucinations but sometimes triggers on borderline cases.

Prototype few-shot sets (compact):
--- EXAMPLES START ---
Input: "Study: 100 participants, shows correlation between A and B (p < .05); details not listed."
Good summary: "Study with 100 participants reports a correlation between A and B; details not provided."
Bad summary: "The study proves A causes B and reports effect size 0.42."

Input: "Short press release: company announces new product; no specs or price."
Null exemplar expected: "NO_SUMMARY_NEEDED"
--- EXAMPLES END ---

Failure cases observed:
- Borderline inference: model still infers directionality (says "A causes B") when only correlation shown. Need stronger contrast or an explicit canonical phrase like "no causal claim" in the pos exemplar.
- Over-application of nullspace: hard token anchor sometimes suppressed useful high-level summaries (false negatives).
- Token budget: when we add 4 negative exemplars the prompt length grows and latency/cost increase; diminishing returns after 2 negatives for our Llama-variant tests.

Mitigation strategies tried: 
- Softening nullspace: use phrase "insufficient detail to summarize" instead of NO_SUMMARY_NEEDED; reduces false negatives but increases residual hallucination.
- Mixed temperature conditioning: set temperature lower (0.0–0.3) when anchor present to favor conservative outputs.
- Post-filter classifier: run a cheap binary classifier to detect hallucination candidate and fallback to NO_SUMMARY_NEEDED — offloads risk from prompt but adds a model hop.

Microtemplates (token-budget conscious) — two variants:
A) Compact contrast (≈ 120 tokens):
"CONTEXT:" <article text>
Task: one-line fact-only summary.
EX1_INPUT: <example1 text>
EX1_OUTPUT: <good>
EX2_INPUT: <ex2 text>
EX2_OUTPUT: <bad>
PROMPT: CONTEXT:

B) Nullspace-light (≈ 90 tokens):
"CONTEXT:" <article>
If article lacks explicit factual details, reply: "insufficient detail to summarize."
Then give example pair and new CONTEXT.

Metrics to track per run: precision_of_named_entities, false_positive_fact_rate, token_cost, latency_95p.

Logging / eval plan:
- Make small eval set of 200 ambiguous blurbs (mix press releases, abstracts, tweets) with human labels: can-summarize / insufficient-detail.
- Run baseline, contrast-1neg, contrast-3neg, null-hard, null-soft. 4 seeds each (temp 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.7).
- Track per-seed metric changes and cost.

Diagnostic heuristics (for debugging prompts):
- Attention probe: replace target with tokenized anchor and see how often token appears in top-k.
- Response length histogram: nullspace tends to produce a spike at ~1–3 tokens — detect and inspect.
- Confusion cases: show where model flips between pos and neg depending on small phrasing changes. Save those for rule/sanitizer creation.

Notes to self:
- Try explicit instruction: "When in doubt, prefer "insufficient detail to summarize"." Might bias too conservative but safer for product.
- Test with Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching/quantization might change behavior (quantization noise could make nullspace anchors brittle). Need to test 4-bit vs 8-bit.
- Slack thread idea: get canonical phrasing for nullspace (Asha volunteered to poll CS). Put final phrasing in product prompt library as "no-op exemplar".

Tickets to create / followups:
- ENG-1423: run batch experiment across 3 model families (open-llama, redwood-curie, redwood-gpt-tier1) — linked above.
- Create small post-filter classifier prototype (PR #87 references).

Random small experiments to run next:
- Contrast with paraphrased neg exemplar (same negative content phrased differently) to force model to learn the *concept* of what to avoid, not surface tokens.
- Use few-token metadata tag in exemplar (e.g. [NEGATIVE_EX]) and see if token-based anchors are more robust than natural-language negatives.
- Combine contrast with explicit step-by-step justification requirement in pos exemplar to increase precision without losing recall.

Scratch list (todo):
- [ ] Build eval set (200 items) + labels (assign to Asha/Miguel)
- [ ] Run null-hard vs null-soft vs baseline across 3 models, capture metrics
- [ ] Draft product-friendly wording for library entry (short, 1-sentence rule + example)
- [ ] Check impact of quantization profiles (8-bit vs 4-bit) on anchor reliability

Random notes / heuristics captured:
- Negative exemplars work best when they mimic the same surface distribution as positives (same length, same register) — otherwise model treats them as outliers.
- Hard token anchors are good for rule enforcement; use sparingly and with fallback detection.
- For few-shot economy, 1 negative exemplar paired with a short nullspace anchor often captures most of the benefit.

References & inspiration (internal):
- internal convo: https://slack-redwood-internal-inference/thread/CB12345 (see Asha comments 2024-09-02)
- jira: ENG-1423 (experiment coord)
- PR draft: https://github.com/redwood-inference/prompt-lab/pull/87 (early post-filter classifier)

Notes end.

Quick export summary (for copying into a ticket):
- Title: Fewshot contrast + nullspace anchors — experiments to reduce hallucinations in short-summary prompts.
- Quick result: 1 negative exemplar + 1 nullspace-hard anchor reduced false-positive fact hallucinations ~35% vs baseline in small pilot; modest increase in false negatives. Need larger eval.

-- Lena
